stem: Hirano bodies seen in which one of the following types of dementia?
explanation: Hirano bodies were first described by Hirano in 1965. These are intracellular eosinophilic rod-shaped structures seen in the neurons of individuals with Alzheimer's and some forms of Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease (Cartier et al., 1985).

stem: Tom is a 12-year-old boy with reduced social interactions, poor communication abilities and repetitive stereotypical behaviour. The macroscopic changes involved in the pathogenesis of this condition would be hypoplasia of the
explanation: Reduced social interactions, poor communication abilities and repetitive stereotypical behaviour are core features of autistic spectrum disorder. In children with autism, hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis and to some extent the cerebellar hemispheres is documented. Purkinje cell count in cerebellum is significantly lower

stem: In CJD, the amyloid plaques are prominent in which part of the brain?
explanation: CJD is a type of multifocal dementia involving the cerebellar structures, where amyloid plaques are prominent.

stem: A 75-year-old gentleman with memory problems, disinhibition and lack of insight. What microscopic findings will be expected in this case?
explanation: This man is exhibiting symptoms of fronto-temporal dementia. The syndrome of FTD has been associated with two types of pathological change, which in individual cases cannot be predicted on clinical grounds. Tau positive inclusions account for the majority of cases, and most familial (but not sporadic) cases with tau pathology carry mutations in the microtubule-associated tau protein on chromosome 17. The other main pathological finding in FTD is so-called ubiquitin-only pathology with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions (i.e. negative for tau or alpha-synuclein), suggesting a link with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

stem: A 37-year-old male presents with episodes of waxing and waning neurological deficits. The most likely pathological change in brain is
explanation: This patient has a diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis. This is caused by the gradual demyelination that leads to delayed and inhibited signal conduction.

stem: Which of the following is least likely to occur in schizophrenia?
explanation: In terms of histological changes, no evidence for astrogliosis in schizophrenia has been reported. Reduced cell numbers or cell size has been described especially affecting neurons in the hippocampus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The Increase in neuronal density, which may relate to the observed decrease in neurone size has been reported. Subtle cytoarchitectural anomalies were described in the hippocampal formation and frontal cortex. Synaptic studies in the hippocampus and DLPFC in schizophrenia show decrements in presynaptic markers. (Ref: Harrison PJ. The neuropathology of schizophrenia. A critical review of the data and their interpretation. Brain 1999; 122: 593-624)

stem: An intravenous heroin user presents with significant slowing of cognitive ability. He has fatuous affect and impaired concentration that has developed insidiously. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
explanation: HIV dementia can present with the above features. See Neuroscience section on HIV

stem: In a patient being evaluated for neuropsychiatric disturbances, CT scan shows atrophy of head of caudate nucleus. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
explanation: Huntington's is characterised by this finding especially in late stages; in Fahr's disease calcified basal ganglia are noted.

stem: Which of the following neuroimaging finding is most suggestive of new variant CJD?
options: Activation of primary auditory cortex on functional MRI
Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan
Increased signal in the pulvinar nucleus of thalamus bilaterally
correctAnswer: Increased signal in the pulvinar nucleus of thalamus bilaterally
explanation: The MRI is the most useful supportive diagnostic test in variant CJD. A characteristic abnormality seen in the posterior thalamic region (pulvinar sign) is highly sensitive and specific for variant CJD.

stem: A patient develops viral encephalitis. He exhibits increased oral exploratory behaviour and inappropriate sexuality. This syndrome can be called
explanation: Hypermetamorphopsia (compulsion to attend to all visual stimuli), hyperorality, hypersexuality, blunted emotional reactivity is called Kluver-Bucy syndrome; the full syndrome is rarely seen in man, but partial syndrome can occur with viral encephalitis affecting temporal lobe.

stem: Which of the following human spongiform encephalopathy has the slowest course?
explanation: Kuru is a type of prion disease which has the slowest course. The incubation period was prolonged- up to 40 years before disease onset, which was then rapid and fatal. It is thought to have been transmitted by ritual cannibalism. Symptoms include personality and behavioural disturbances, progressive cerebellar ataxia, dementia and death.

stem: Mr. X is a 73-year-old gentleman with 5-year history of Parkinson's disease, cognitive decline and visual hallucinations. Post mortem evidence suggests alpha syn-nuclein deposits and cytoplasmic inclusions. The common microscopic finding expected in this case would be
explanation: The clinical features, in this case, are suggestive of Parkinson's disease dementia. In Parkinson's disease, the Lewy bodies are confined to the substantia nigra. The Lewy bodies are weak eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusions. Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia contains an accumulation of alpha-synuclein and is classified under synucleinopathies.

stem: Which of the following neuroimaging finding is most suggestive of Alzheimer's disease?
options: Activation of primary auditory cortex on functional MRI
Increased signal in the Pulvinar nucleus of thalamus bilaterally
Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan
correctAnswer: Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan
explanation: MRI often shows atrophy of grey matter involving the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe.
